---
title: "Translating from scipy.special"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

zuspecial evaluates `scipy.special`'s functions with the C++ kernels
SciPy itself uses: [xsf](https://github.com/scipy/xsf) at the commit SciPy
1.18.1 vendors, and Boost.Math for the six functions SciPy evaluates with
it. This article is for readers who know `scipy.special` and want to move
code between the two: what carries over unchanged, what R does
differently, and the few places zuspecial departs from SciPy on purpose.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zuspecial)
```

## Names and arguments

Every function is `sc_` followed by its SciPy name, and takes SciPy's
arguments in SciPy's order. A line of Python

```python
import scipy.special as sc
sc.gammainc(2, 3)
```

becomes

```{r}
sc_gammainc(2, 3)
```

Base R often puts the same arguments the other way round. `pgamma()` is
the regularised lower incomplete gamma function too, with the argument
first and the shape second:

```{r}
pgamma(3, 2)
```

The same holds for the Bessel functions: `sc_jv(v, z)` against
`besselJ(x, nu)`. Each help page names the base R and `gsl` counterparts.

Two functions take an argument SciPy spells as a separate keyword or
function, both as in SciPy's Python wrappers: `sc_zeta(x, q = NULL)` is
the Riemann zeta function without `q` and the Hurwitz zeta function with
it, and the spherical Bessel functions take `derivative = FALSE`.

```{r}
sc_zeta(2)
sc_zeta(2, q = 2)
sc_spherical_jn(1, 2, derivative = TRUE)
```

`zuspecial_info()$functions` lists the `r nrow(zuspecial_info()$functions)`
functions with their backend and whether they take complex arguments.

## Real and complex arguments

A function SciPy registers for complex input takes the complex path when
its argument is of type `complex`, and returns `complex`. A real argument
stays on the real path and returns `double`, so, as in SciPy, there is no
automatic promotion when the real result is undefined:

```{r}
sc_jv(0.5, -1)
sc_jv(0.5, -1 + 0i)
```

R's `c()` makes a whole vector complex once one element is, so mixing the
two in one vector sends every element down the complex path. Keep real and
complex inputs in separate vectors when the distinction matters.

Integer arguments (`n` in `sc_expn()` and the spherical Bessel functions,
`k` in `sc_lambertw()`) must hold whole numbers within R's integer range.
Integer and logical vectors are converted to double; character, factor,
list and classed input (dates, difftimes) is refused.

## Vectorisation

zuspecial's functions are vectorised like R's arithmetic, not broadcast
like NumPy's ufuncs:

* Length-one arguments recycle against the others. Any other mismatch in
  length is an error of class `zuspecial_recycle_error`, never a warning:
  a silently recycled parameter vector is a bug.
* Arrays are not broadcast. Where NumPy turns a `(2, 1)` array and a
  `(3,)` array into a `(2, 3)` result, R needs `outer()`:

  ```{r}
  outer(0:1, 1:3, sc_jv)
  ```

* The result keeps `dim` and `dimnames` from the first full-length
  argument that has them, otherwise `names`, as base R does:

  ```{r}
  sc_gamma(c(a = 0.5, b = 5))
  ```

## Missing values

R has `NA` as well as `NaN`, and keeps them apart. `NA` in any argument
gives `NA` in that element, decided before the kernel is called; `NaN`
goes to the kernel and gives what SciPy gives, normally `NaN`:

```{r}
sc_gamma(c(NA, NaN, 3))
```

A complex element is `NA` when either part is. A multi-output function
returns `NA` in every output for that element.

## Floating-point conditions

xsf reports a pole, an overflow or a loss of precision through SciPy's ten
error codes: `singular`, `underflow`, `overflow`, `slow`, `loss`,
`no_result`, `domain`, `arg`, `other` and `memory`. As in SciPy, every code
is ignored by default except `memory`:

```{r}
sc_geterr()
```

`sc_seterr()` and `sc_errstate()` are `scipy.special.seterr()` and
`scipy.special.errstate()`. `sc_errstate()` takes the expression first,
where Python uses a `with` block:

```python
with sc.errstate(singular="raise"):
    sc.gamma(-1)
```

```{r}
tryCatch(
  sc_errstate(sc_gamma(-1), singular = "raise"),
  zuspecial_singular_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

Three things differ from SciPy:

* A code is signalled once per call, with the number of elements that
  raised it and the index of the first, not once per element.
* Only the codes the kernels report are signalled. SciPy also turns the
  processor's floating-point flags into codes, so it raises a few that
  zuspecial does not, such as `overflow` for `exp1(800)`. The values are
  the same.
* Warnings and errors are R conditions with classes
  (`zuspecial_warning`, `zuspecial_<code>`, `zuspecial_error`,
  `zuspecial_<code>_error`), for `tryCatch()` and
  `withCallingHandlers()`.

The state is stored in the option `zuspecial.errstate`, so parallel R
workers start from the defaults rather than inheriting the parent's.

## Functions with several outputs

Where SciPy returns a tuple, zuspecial returns a named list, with the names
SciPy's documentation uses:

```python
ai, aip, bi, bip = sc.airy(1)
```

```{r}
airy <- sc_airy(1)
airy$bi
names(sc_ellipj(0.5, 0.3))
```

## From compiled code

Packages that need these functions from C or C++ can call 32 of them, the
complex `jv` among them, through a registered table, without linking to xsf
or Boost. Add zuspecial to `Imports` and `LinkingTo` in `DESCRIPTION`,
import something from it in `NAMESPACE` so that its namespace loads (for
example `importFrom(zuspecial, zuspecial_info)`), and then:

```c
#include <R.h>
#include <R_ext/Rdynload.h>
#define ZUSPECIAL_DEFINE_API_GET
#include <zuspecial.h>

double gamma_or_nan(double x) {
  const zuspecial_api *api = zuspecial_api_get();
  int code;
  double value = api->gamma(x, &code);
  return code == 0 ? value : R_NaN;
}
```

Each member evaluates one element, exactly as the R function does, and
reports the lowest-numbered error code the evaluation raised in `code`
(0 when none). `sc_seterr()` does not apply: the caller decides what a code
means. The members are reentrant and safe from any thread. The header,
`inst/include/zuspecial.h`, documents the members and how the table is
versioned.

## Where zuspecial differs from SciPy

* **`sc_expn()` with a non-whole `n`.** SciPy truncates it with a
  `RuntimeWarning`; zuspecial refuses it. A `NaN` `n` gives `NaN` in both.
* **Arguments beyond about 1e5 on Windows.** R on Windows is built with
  Rtools, whose C library (mingw-w64 v11) evaluates `sin()` and `cos()`
  inaccurately for large arguments, as base R's own `sin()` shows. Kernels
  that take the sine or cosine of such a value are less accurate there than
  on Linux and macOS. The affected help pages have a "Windows" section.
* **Functions not yet included.** Version 0.1.0 covers the gamma, beta,
  error, exponential-integral, Bessel, Airy, hypergeometric, elliptic,
  zeta and Struve families. The Carlson elliptic integrals wait for a SciPy release
  whose xsf has them; Kelvin, Mathieu, spheroidal, parabolic-cylinder,
  Fresnel, Legendre and the orthogonal polynomials come later.
  Single precision, arbitrary precision and the distribution families of
  `scipy.stats` are out of scope.

## How the values are checked

Every function with a table in [xsref](https://github.com/scipy/xsref),
SciPy's mpmath reference collection, is checked against it on Linux, macOS
and Windows, with xsf's own error metric and tolerances. The functions are
also compared with values computed by SciPy 1.18.1 on each platform, and
with the `gsl`, `Bessel`, `hypergeo`, `lamW`, `expint` and `Rmpfr`
packages. `zuspecial_info()` reports the xsf, SciPy, xsref and Boost
versions the installed package was built from.

## Speed

The R layer adds about 10 % to the kernel's time on 10 000 elements and
nothing measurable beyond 100 000. Against base R on real input,
`sc_gamma()` and `sc_gammaln()` are at least as fast as `gamma()` and `lgamma()`,
and `sc_jv()` takes about 2.7 times as long as `besselJ()`: the time is
xsf's kernel, which is also SciPy's. On complex input `sc_jv()` is several
times faster than `Bessel::BesselJ()`. `tools/run-benchmarks` in the
source repository reproduces these figures.
